title: Vibrotactile stimulation of the larynx for refractory chronic cough
text:
Chronic cough that does not respond to standard cough treatments (known as refractory chronic cough) is
highly disruptive and significantly reduces well-being. The proposed studies will lay the groundwork for a larger
clinical trial of the use of vibrotactile stimulation to the larynx to reduce refractory chronic cough via dose
refinement (Aim 1) and conduct of a pilot randomized clinical trial (Aim 2). This potential treatment is
noninvasive, repeatable, independently usable, and portable, making it a promising option for improving the
quality of life of people who suffer from refractory chronic cough.

title: Interacting Partners of Bestrophin Channels
text:
Bestrophins are a family of ion channels with critical (patho)physiological roles in the eye, as mutations of
bestrophin-1 (Best1) cause retinal degenerative disorders, while bestrophin-2 (Best2) regulates intra-ocular
pressure. This project is aimed to identify interacting protein partners of bestrophins and elucidate the structural
and functional consequences of these interactions. The findings from this work will provide important knowledge
on ocular physiology, and establish a versatile platform for investigating other ion channels of interest and their
interacting partners.

title: The Role of Dentate Spikes in Cognition and Epilepsy
text:
Synchronization of neural activity within and across brain regions is critical for cognition and is often disrupted
in neurological diseases like temporal lobe epilepsy that coincide with significant cognitive impairment. Dentate
spikes are large amplitude events that are hypothesized to synchronize neural activity across the brain, but
their direct role in cognition and neurological disease remains unclear. This proposal will use neural recordings
and optogenetics to investigate how dentate spikes drive synchronized neural activity in hippocampus and
medial entorhinal cortex and determine how alterations to dentate spikes impact cognitive deficits in epilepsy.

title: Exploiting the Cross-talk between Neurotrophin Receptors and Mixed Lineage Kinases to Target Pancreatic Cancer.
text:
The incidence of certain types of cancer, including pancreatic cancer (PDAC), is higher in veterans. Several
reports suggest an increased risk of PDAC in veterans deployed to Vietnam during the war. It is predicted that
by 2030, the PDAC incidence and mortality will be the second-highest, and thus, it is necessary to identify new
targets and drugs. Our group has been working on a novel group of kinases called Mixed Lineage Kinases
(MLKs), and recently, we reported that a pan-MLK inhibitor decreased the PDAC tumor burden and extended
the life of animals. Moreover, our new data suggest that the action of pan-MLK inhibitor in cancer is dependent
on the neurotrophin receptor TrkA, which plays a central role in neuropathic pain. The pan-Trk inhibitors are in
clinical use for various solid cancers. Our preliminary data show that combining pan-MLK and pan-Trk inhibitors
is more effective than the single agent in the PDAC mouse model. The combination therapy extended the life of
PDAC animals more than the single agent. We expect to take our discoveries to clinical trials in the future.

title: Next generation T cell therapies for mutant KRAS solid tumors
text:
Our goal is to develop the next generation of T cell therapies for adult solid tumors. Recent advances in CRISPR-
Cas9 technology allow investigators to design better and safer T cell products for adoptive cell therapy. An
outstanding team of investigators has been assembled to develop a new TCR-T cell therapy directed to mutant
KRAS that overcomes the critical challenges posed by the tumor microenvironment and T cell exhaustion.
Laboratory correlatives using state-of-the art single cell technologies will be employed to investigate mechanisms
of response and resistance after treatment. In this personalized medicine-based strategy, we estimate that 5,000
new adult cancer patients in the US per year will be eligible for this cell therapy.

title: Identifying molecular vulnerabilities of ALT-dependent cancers
text:
5%-10% of human cancers rely on the alternative lengthening of telomere (ALT)-based mechanism for telomere
elongation. We aim to elucidate the molecular cascades underlying the ALT-directed telomere maintenance. We
will identify the critical dependencies and novel mechanistic-driven therapeutic targets against ALT-dependent
human cancers including ATRX mutant malignant gliomas.

title: EGF Receptor Endocytosis: Mechanisms and Role in Signaling
text:
The Administrative supplement is requested to enable uniform image illumination of the field of view of the
spinning disk confocal imaging system to study the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling. EGFR
plays an important role in mammalian development, wound healing, tissue regeneration and tissue
homeostasis in the adult. EGFR is also involved in various cell abnormalities, most notably, tumorigenesis and
metastatic processes. The mechanisms regulating EGFR signaling are incompletely understood. The proposed
research will address the fundamental question of how multiple intertwining signaling pathways activated by
EGFR are regulated by the subcellular localization of the constituents of those pathways.

title: Screening for small-molecule inhibitors of respiratory syncytial viral infection in infant bronchial epithelial barrier
text:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) can cause severe infection mostly in children younger than 2 years of age,
at least in part due to their impaired bronchial epithelial cell responses to RSV. Leveraging established RSV
infection models, we propose a high-throughput screening for compounds that reduce RSV infection in infant
bronchial epithelial cells as potential therapeutics.

title: Core C: Cell Phenotyping and Molecular Imaging Core
text:
The overarching goal this P01 proposal to better understand mechanisms in the core Cyclin D-Cdk4/6-Rb-E2F
pathway regulating the G1/S transition controlling human cell division to facilitate development of novel cancer
therapeutics. To test these hypotheses, all projects will rely on the cell phenotyping and molecular imaging
core to generate mutations and analyze their effects on cell cycle progression and protein interactions. To
support the program projects, this core aims to 1) use CRIPSR/Cas9 genome editing to generate mutant cell
lines; 2) image gene expression, cell growth, and cell cycle transition dynamics at single cell resolution; and 3)
build and maintain software that analyzes the terabytes of time lapse imaging data.

title: Core B - Instrumentation
text:
CORE B – PROJECT NARRATIVE
The Instrumentation and Imaging Core (Core B) provides shared instrumentation and high-resolution imaging
services needed for the success of all Projects in this program. The core also coordinates maintenance and
training, and aims to advance the development of new, innovative tools for understanding the replication cycles
of cancer-associated viruses and how they cause human diseases.

title: COBRE in Digestive and Liver Disease - Imaging Core
text: Advanced Imaging Core – Project Summary The COBRE in Digestive & Liver Disease (CDLD) Advanced Imaging Core provides equipment, expertise, and training to CDLD investigators for state-of-the-art cell- and tissue-based imaging, including confocal, multiphoton and super-resolution microscopy of live and fixed cells and tissues, intravital imaging and automated imaging of histological slides. The Advanced Imaging Core houses the following major microscope systems: 1) Leica Stellaris 8 tauSTED Xtend Super-Resolution Microscope; 2) Andor BC43 Spinning Disk Confocal Microscope; 3) Zeiss LSM 880 NLO confocal/multiphoton microscope with Fast Airyscan super-resolution and Quasar spectral detectors; 4) Olympus FluoView 1200 MPE Intravital Microscope; 5) Olympus FluoView Fv10i confocal microscope; 6) Leica TCS SP8 laser scanning confocal microscope; and 7) BD Biosciences CARV II real-time spinning disk confocal microscope; 8) Zeiss LSM 510 META confocal; 9) Perkin-Elmer Vectra Polaris automated quantitative pathology imaging system; 10) Zeiss Axiovert 200M microscope; and 11) Agilent Cytation 5 Cell Imaging Multi-Mode Reader. Except for Vectra Polaris which is customized for histological slides, all microscopes are equipped with environmental chambers for temperature and gas phase control to allow non-destructive 3D imaging of living cells, tissues and organisms. Major applications include 1) live cell imaging of parameter- sensitive fluorophores to monitor ions, electrical potentials, radical generation, pyridine nucleotide reduction, membrane permeability, cell viability (apoptosis and necrosis), and the submicron distribution of fluorescent proteins and other fluorescent reporters; 2) high resolution imaging of tissue sections for immunocytochemistry and fluorescent protein distribution; 3) fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) and DuoLink to characterize and quantify interactions between specific molecules; 4) intravital microscopy to monitor microcirculation, leukocyte margination, mitochondrial polarization and permeability, radical generation, gene expression and other parameters in living animals; and 5) high throughput, quantitative multiplexed imaging of conventionally and immunostained clinical and research specimens. Ancillary equipment required for specimen preparation is also provided. Consultation and services for TEM and SEM are available through the Department of Pathology & Laboratory Medicine. Computer workstations provide offline image processing/analysis (ImageJ FIJI, Metamorph, IPLab and other software). Advanced Imaging Core services provide training and assistance to promote the success of individual CDLD investigators.

title: Biomarkers to stratify pain severity and type in pancreatic disease
text:
Most patients with chronic pancreatitis experience severely debilitating pain. Unfortunately, only ~25% of these
chronic pancreatitis patients achieve meaningful pain relief with current standard of care for pain management,
highlighting the urgent need for objective biomarkers to stratify pain type and pain severity. This proposal is
designed to discover (Specific Aims 1 and 2) and validate (Specific Aims 3 and 4) such pain biomarkers in
plasma and/or urine, which have the potential to significantly improve pain management for chronic pancreatitis
patients so that the majority can enjoy a meaningful pain relief.

title: Targeted radiation and immunocytokine therapy for CEA positive malignancies
text:
Sequential therapy of solid tumors with tumor targeted radiation therapy followed by untargeted immune
therapy has shown promise in the clinic. This approach can be further improved by using targeted immune
therapy and studying the immune response on tumor biopsies taken before and after therapy. Using a
combination of clinical and animal model data, we will refine the therapeutic doses and identify the best
predictive markers of response to therapy.

title: Spatiotemporal regulation of neurotransmission at single synapses
text:
This proposal leverages the power of iGluSnFR3, a third-generation glutamate-sensing fluorescent reporter, to
directly visualize asynchronous neurotransmitter release at the quantal level. Through two complementary yet
independent aims, I will investigate a range of molecular and physiological drivers to test the hypothesis that
asynchronous neurotransmission represents a distinct signaling pathway, separate from other modes of
neurotransmitter release, with unique regulatory mechanisms and downstream functional outcomes. These
findings will provide critical insights into synaptic processes that shape neuronal communication and information
processing in the central nervous system.

title: Identifying autism motor deficits in infants using computer vision
text:
Infant motor deficits have an as yet unfulfilled potential for predicting later autism diagnosis. To address this,
we will apply advanced techniques in machine learning to predict autism diagnosis and severity in an existing
set of screening videos of infants at increased familial likelihood of ASD. By demonstrating the potential of
these techniques on this dataset, this work will open the door to automated, scalable prediction of autism
diagnosis and severity from a wide range of naturalistic video data.

title: Characterizing human-microbiome interactions via molecular and functional genomic approaches
text:
While it is clear that the microbiota play a key role in human health, we lack an understanding of the
physiological processes that determine microbiota composition across the body. To address this gap, the the
goals of this proposal are to i) identify relationships between host genes and mucosal bacteria and archaea, ii)
identify non-prokaryotic elements of the human microbiome associated with human gene expression and ii)
demonstrate causal relationships between the microbiome and host gene expression. Ultimately, the results of
this project will inform our understanding of the relationship between the microbiota and host in health and
disease and highlight areas of interest for novel, microbiome-based therapeutics.

title: Heartland Cancer Research NCORP
text:
The Heartland Cancer Research NCORP (Heartland NCORP) will be the premier community cancer research organization
of the states of Illinois and Missouri by providing state of the art cancer clinical trials, cancer care delivery research,
interdisciplinary cancer treatment planning, and coordinated biomarker driven research throughout our service region.
Cancer patients, in specific, will benefit as a direct result of these clinical trials, and the consequential knowledge on
preventing and treating malignancy in community settings will improve patient care.

title: Genetic and Epigenetic Determinants of Longevity
text:
How well organisms age and how long they live critically depend on their genetic make-up, their life history,
and their environmental exposures. This application proposes to use the powerful genetic model C. elegans to
investigate how the genome and the environment interact to regulate gene expression, which plays a profound
role in aging trajectories. This proposal aims to gain molecular insights into how stress exposures and major
regulators can be managed/manipulated to achieve healthy aging, with a particular focus on key players that
are evolutionarily highly conserved, leading to findings that are likely readily translatable and relevant to aging
research in humans.

title: Tissue-Specific Modulation of mtDNA Mutations: Exploring Aging and Lifestyle Interventions
text:
The research proposal aims to investigate how mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations contribute to aging and
age-related diseases, focusing on tissue-specific accumulation and clearance of these mutations. The study will
use mouse models to assess the effects of exercise and calorie restriction on mtDNA mutations and explore how
the timing of these mutations impacts aging. The goal is to identify mechanisms that could lead to targeted
interventions to mitigate age-related diseases and improve healthspan.

title: Nanotechnology-based cardiovascular vaccines
text:
4Narrative3
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the number one cause of death worldwide. The main drugs used for CVD
management are statins, but they have side effects, must be taken as a lifelong therapy, and there is a lack of
patient compliance in primary prevention. We propose an active immunotherapy approach to CVD to protect
from onset of atherosclerosis or progression to thrombosis – if successful this would have an immense positive
impact on human health.
